summary: Describes how Novell IPX operates over various WAN media, including the IPXWAN protocol Novell uses to exchange router-to-router information before using the link for IPX routing. It was replaced by RFC 1634.

eli5.summary: Two Novell routers meeting over a long cable first swap a few facts, like a handshake, so they can then pass traffic properly.

questions: how does ipx set up wan connections
what is link master and slave
how is link delay calculated in ipxwan
what is the difference between primary and link network numbers
subtitle: How Novell IPX routers exchange link information before using a WAN connection

tldr.problem: Novell IPX routers need to exchange information before they can route traffic over WAN links, but IPX is designed for LANs and different WAN technologies have different link-establishment procedures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1362 defines the IPXWAN protocol, a handshake where routers send timer packets to measure link delay, exchange routing capabilities, and establish a shared network number before standard IPX routing begins.
tldr.outcome: IPX can operate uniformly over diverse WAN media (PPP, X.25, Frame Relay) with a single negotiation protocol. RFC 1634 later replaced it.

today: RFC 1634 replaced RFC 1362 as the specification for Novell IPX over WAN media.

sections.title: The Handshake Problem
sections.content:
Novell IPX is a connectionless datagram protocol designed for local area networks where link establishment is instantaneous. However, wide area networks often require explicit connection setup, and different WAN technologies have different procedures: PPP (point-to-point protocol) needs NCP negotiation, X.25 requires virtual circuit establishment, and Frame Relay has permanent or switched virtual circuits. Before exchanging routing information, IPX routers must first negotiate over these diverse links.

RFC 1362 solves this by defining a common IPXWAN protocol that both routers run immediately after the link layer comes up, regardless of the underlying WAN medium. This protocol lets routers exchange timing and routing information before standard IPX routing begins.
sections.eli5: IPX was built for fast local networks. WAN links are slower and need setup. IPXWAN is a quick conversation two routers have when they first meet on a WAN link, so they know how to talk before real traffic flows.

sections.title: The Link Negotiation Process
sections.content:
IPXWAN defines two roles: link master and link slave. After link establishment, both routers send Timer Request packets every 20 seconds until receiving a response or timing out (typically one minute). When a router receives a Timer Request, the router with the lower primary network number becomes the slave and responds with a Timer Response packet.

The master measures the round-trip time between Timer Request and Timer Response to calculate link delay in milliseconds. The master then assigns a common network number (unique across the network) and sends an Information Request packet containing this number, the calculated delay, and its router name. The slave echoes back an Information Response with its own router name. Once both sides have exchanged this information, they begin standard IPX RIP (routing information protocol) and SAP (service advertisement protocol) traffic.
sections.eli5: The router with the smaller network ID becomes the boss and measures the link's speed. It picks a shared network number and tells the other router. Both sides agree, then normal routing starts.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
All IPXWAN packets are IPX packet type 04 (Packet Exchange) using reserved socket number 0x9004. All packets are always 576 bytes (the maximum IPX size) to prevent compression modems from distorting delay calculations.

Timer Request and Timer Response packets contain a WIdentifier field (0x5741534D, the ASCII code for WASM) to identify IPXWAN packets, a WPacket Type field (0 for request, 1 for response), and the sender's primary network number (WNode ID). The WSequence field starts at 0 and increments with each retry; only responses matching the sequence number are accepted. Both packet types include two options: one defining the routing type (currently only 0 for IPX RIP/SAP) and a padding option that fills the packet with a repeating 0x00-0xFF pattern.

Information Request and Information Response packets (used only when routing type is 0) carry the link delay (in milliseconds, calculated from the timer exchange), the common network number, and a 48-byte router name field padded with nulls.
sections.eli5: Packets are always 576 bytes and start with a special code word so routers know they are IPXWAN messages. They say which router sent it, how fast the link is, and a shared network number the master picked.

sections.title: Network Organization and Protocol Support
sections.content:
Every IPXWAN router has a primary network number, a unique 32-bit identifier assigned to the router itself (analogous to an internal network number in NetWare). Each router also has a router name, a symbolic 1- to 47-character identifier used for management and display purposes.

The IPXWAN protocol is extensible through router type options. Routing type 0 (IPX RIP/SAP with a link network number) is the minimum interoperability requirement, and all implementations must support it. Vendors can define additional routing types by obtaining numbers from Novell; these appear as WOption fields in the Timer Request packet. Multiple routing types can be negotiated, with the slave selecting which type to use based on its capabilities.
sections.eli5: Each router has a unique network ID number and a friendly name. IPXWAN can be extended to support different routing methods by adding new option types, but all routers must at least support the basic IPX RIP/SAP routing.
